title: The Ottoman Centuries
tagline: The Ottoman state from a frontier beylik in Anatolia to the Republic of Turkey.
intro: The Ottoman Empire lasted over six centuries, from about 1299 to 1922, and at its height ruled across three continents. These stops follow it from Osman I's beylik on the Byzantine frontier through the conquest of Constantinople, the gains of Selim I and the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent. They then turn to the reforms of the nineteenth century, the Tanzimat and the Young Turks, and to the defeat in the First World War that ended the sultanate in 1922. The last stops show the Republic proclaimed in Ankara in 1923 under Mustafa Kemal.

steps.why: A frontier beylik in Anatolia grew, with Janissary infantry, gunpowder artillery and a sophisticated bureaucracy, into a power spanning three continents for six centuries.
Osman I, a Turkoman chieftain of the Kayı clan, held a beylik in Bithynia on the Byzantine frontier, and his victory at Bapheus in 1301 gave the dynasty its military credibility.
In 1453 Mehmed II took the Byzantine capital after a siege in which heavy artillery played a major role, ending the Byzantine Empire and making the city the Ottoman capital.
Selim I defeated the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514 and conquered the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516–1517, bringing Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia under Ottoman rule.
Suleiman, known in Turkish as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, conquered Belgrade, won at Mohács and besieged Vienna, in a reign treated as the height of Ottoman power and legal codification.
First recruited from Christian boys through the devshirme, the elite infantry became one of Europe's first standing armies to use firearms on a large scale, until their abolition in 1826.
From the Edict of Gülhane in 1839 to the constitution of 1876, Ottoman statesmen rebuilt the ministries, courts, schools, law codes and army and promised equality to all subjects.
Their Committee of Union and Progress forced the sultan to restore the constitution in 1908, later ruled as a dictatorship and masterminded the genocides of Ottoman Christians.
After the Ottoman defeat and the Allied occupation of Istanbul, Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman army officer, led the Turkish national movement against the post-war partition of Anatolia.
Proclaimed in Ankara on 29 October 1923 after the Treaty of Lausanne, the Republic was turned by Mustafa Kemal's reforms into a secular nation state with a new civil code and alphabet.

title: Russia from Rus' to Revolution
tagline: The Russian state from the princes of Kiev to the Soviet Union and its end.
intro: The first great East Slavic state was Kievan Rus', ruled by the Rurikid princes from Kiev on the river route from the Baltic to Byzantium. These stops follow its conversion to Orthodox Christianity, the merchant republic of Novgorod, the Mongol conquest and the rise of Moscow, which gathered the Russian lands and threw off Tatar rule. They continue through the tsars from Ivan IV to Peter the Great, the Russian Empire that grew to some 22.8 million square kilometres, and the revolution of 1917. The last stop is the Soviet Union, founded in 1922 and dissolved in 1991.

steps.why: Rurikid princes ruled the first great East Slavic state from Kiev, a federation of principalities on the river route from the Baltic to Byzantium, until the Mongols sacked Kiev in 1240.
In 988 Vladimir the Great accepted Christianity from Byzantium and married the emperor's sister Anna, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art to Kievan Rus'.
This merchant city-state of the Russian north elected its officials and archbishop, hired princes by contract and traded furs with the Hanseatic League until Ivan III annexed it in 1478.
Batu Khan's conquest of 1237–1240 destroyed Ryazan, Vladimir and many other cities, and the Rus' principalities then paid tribute to the Golden Horde for some two centuries.
A small appanage on the Moskva River grew rich collecting tribute for the Golden Horde, ended Tatar overlordship at the Ugra River in 1480 and annexed Novgorod and Tver.
Founded when Ivan IV was crowned the first Tsar of All Russia in 1547, the Tsardom conquered the Volga khanates and crossed Siberia to the Pacific.
Proclaimed emperor in 1721 after victory over Sweden, Peter reorganised the army, built a navy, founded St Petersburg and subordinated the Church to the state.
Grown to some 22.8 million square kilometres from the Baltic to the Pacific, the empire freed some 23 million serfs in 1861 by Alexander II's Emancipation Edict.
The February Revolution of 1917 forced Nicholas II to abdicate, and in the October Revolution the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power, then won the civil war that followed.
Founded in 1922 as the first communist state, it industrialised under Stalin at enormous human cost, rivalled the United States as a superpower and was dissolved in 1991.

title: Nations Born in the Nineteenth Century
tagline: How nationalism, revolts and wars of unification made new states in Europe and the Americas.
intro: Nationalism holds that a nation should govern itself, and scholars frequently date its beginning to the late eighteenth century. These stops follow states made in the nineteenth century: in the Americas, Gran Colombia and the Brazilian Empire, which ended Spanish and Portuguese rule; in Europe, Greece, the first nation state carved from the Ottoman Empire, and Belgium, which broke away from the Netherlands in 1830. The revolutions of 1848 sought nation states across the continent, and the path ends with the kingdom of Italy proclaimed in 1861 and the German Empire in 1871.

steps.why: The ideology that a nation should govern itself and is the only rightful source of political power is frequently dated by scholars to the late 18th century.
Proclaimed by Simón Bolívar's Congress of Angostura in 1819, this republic of Venezuela, New Granada, Quito and Panama ended Spanish rule in South America at Junín and Ayacucho in 1824.
Prince Pedro declared Brazil independent of Portugal in 1822 and ruled it as Emperor Pedro I, founding the only lasting empire in the Americas, which fell to an army coup in 1889.
A revolt against Ottoman rule in the 1820s ended with international recognition of an independent Greek state in 1830, after European powers intervened decisively on the Greek side.
Created by Britain, France and Russia in 1832 with Otto of Bavaria as king, it was the first nation state carved from the Ottoman Empire and pursued the Great Idea of uniting all Greeks.
Riots in Brussels after an opera in August 1830 led the southern provinces to break away from William I of the Netherlands, and the great powers recognised Belgium in 1831.
The springtime of the peoples spread from Sicily and Paris to more than fifty countries, as workers and middle-class reformers sought constitutions, nation states and a free press.
In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi led the Expedition of the Thousand that conquered Sicily and Naples, a decisive step in the unification of Italy.
Parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II king of Italy in 1861, and the House of Savoy completed unification when Italian troops took Rome from the Papal States in 1870.
Proclaimed at Versailles in 1871 after victory over France, it united the German states under Prussian leadership and became continental Europe's leading industrial power.

title: Inventions That Changed the World
tagline: From the wheel and cuneiform to printing, steam power and the electric telegraph.
intro: The oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement dates from before 4000 BCE, and the speakers of Sumerian developed cuneiform writing around 3200 BCE. These stops follow inventions from those beginnings through paper, the magnetic compass and movable type, all developed in China, to Gutenberg's press in fifteenth-century Europe. They continue with the new instruments of the Scientific Revolution and with the steam engine, made practical for industry by James Watt's separate condenser, and end with the telegraph of the nineteenth century. Where the entries name the makers, they are stops of their own.

steps.why: Miniature clay wheels from north of the Black Sea, from before 4000 BCE, are the oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement; the spoked wheel later allowed swifter war chariots.
Speakers of Sumerian, with Egyptian one of the two earliest written languages, developed cuneiform around 3200 BCE, at first to keep accounts, on tablets written at Uruk.
In 105 CE this court eunuch of the Eastern Han presented Emperor He with paper made from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets, cheaper than silk and lighter than bamboo.
Developed in China, the magnetised needle was used for navigation at sea under the Song Dynasty, aided maritime trade and later transformed navigation worldwide.
Around 1040 CE this Song Dynasty artisan invented movable type printing with ceramic characters, a method recorded by the scholar Shen Kuo, about four centuries before Gutenberg.
In the fifteenth century Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type in Europe, and his press transformed the spread of knowledge there.
From Copernicus in 1543 to Newton in 1687, European scholars joined mathematics, measurement and experiment and used new instruments such as the telescope, microscope and air pump.
Jerónimo de Ayanz patented a steam-powered mine pump in 1606, and Thomas Newcomen's engine of about 1712 was the first commercially successful one to transmit continuous power.
James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769, greatly reduced fuel use, and with Matthew Boulton at Birmingham from 1775 he built engines that drove mills and pumped mines.
Developed in the nineteenth century, the telegraph sent messages by electrical signals along wires, and submarine cables linked Britain with India, Australia and other parts of its empire.
